heroLead: Stronach is a small unincorporated spot on the Manistee River, and the mineral ownership around it usually traces back to old timber and farm land that got split off long before anyone thought about drilling.
intro: Manistee County isn't the Antrim core, and if you own minerals near Stronach you've probably noticed your interest doesn't behave like the gas wells your cousin up in Kalkaska talks about. This part of the state sits in the broader Michigan Basin, where oil and gas history goes back to shallow Dundee limestone production and scattered exploration rather than one dominant shale play. What that means for you: the value of your interest depends heavily on what's actually been drilled near your specific parcel, not on a blanket county story.
We buy mineral and royalty interests around Stronach and the rest of Manistee County. If you're not sure whether what you've got is even active, we'll help you figure that out before talking numbers.

sections.heading: Manistee County Geology Isn't One Simple Story
paragraphs: The Michigan Basin runs deep and wide under this whole region, and Manistee County has seen a mix of activity over the decades — shallow Dundee limestone oil production going back generations, some Antrim gas exploration on the fringe of the core play to the northeast, and Niagaran reef trend potential that runs in a band through parts of the state without hitting every township evenly. Stronach itself, sitting near the Manistee River and inside the Manistee National Forest boundary, has seen less concentrated drilling than the Antrim core counties.
That doesn't mean your interest is worthless — it means the honest answer is usually 'it depends on your specific unit or lease history,' not a flat number quoted off the county name alone.

sections.heading: A Lot of This Ownership Is Legacy, Not Active
paragraphs: Plenty of the mineral interests we come across near Stronach were severed from the surface decades ago when timber or farm land changed hands, and the minerals just got passed down as a line item in an estate nobody paid much attention to. Some of these interests are held by lease with no current production; others produce a small royalty from an old well that's been quietly running for years.

If yours isn't currently producing, it may still have value depending on nearby activity and whether it's held by a lease that could see renewed interest. We'll tell you honestly if there's nothing to price yet — we're not going to pretend a dormant interest is worth more than it is.

sections.heading: Title and Access Out Here
paragraphs: A good chunk of the land around Stronach borders state and national forest ground, and old severed mineral deeds in this area can be thin on detail — sometimes just a legal description and a name, no clear tie to a current parcel number. The Manistee County register of deeds is where that gets sorted out, and it's worth doing before you try to sell, lease, or even just confirm what you own.

If you've got an old deed with a legal description you can't make sense of, send it over. We deal with this kind of paper regularly and can usually tell you fast whether it maps to an active lease or unit.

faqs.question: Is there active oil and gas production near Stronach?
faqs.answer: It varies by parcel. This part of Manistee County has seen scattered Dundee limestone and Antrim-fringe activity, not a dense continuous field, so we check your specific location before saying anything definite.

faqs.question: What if my mineral interest isn't currently producing?
faqs.answer: It may still hold value if it's under lease or near active drilling, but a dormant interest with no nearby activity may have limited near-term value. We'll be straight with you either way.

faqs.question: My deed only has a legal description, no parcel number. Can you still help?
faqs.answer: Yes. Send us what you have. We work with old legal descriptions regularly and can usually match it to current county records.
